He carries the invisible weight of the end-user on his shoulders, fiercely defending the exhausted nurse navigating a delayed schedule or the frantic father buying a midnight fare. They are his unseen congregation, and their seamless experience is his absolute devotion. He speaks of accessibility with a hushed, almost religious fervor, treating friction in design not as a mere technical flaw, but as a profound moral failing. 

Yet, this blinding piety creates a perilous echo chamber. When Elias presents his exhaustive user-advocacy models to the oversight committee, his earnestness floods the room, leaving little space for oxygen, let alone debate. He habitually mistakes the boardroom’s glazed, polite quiet for profound consensus. Because his cause feels so self-evidently righteous, it never occurs to him that his colleagues aren't rendered speechless by shared conviction, but rather subdued by apathy or quietly calculating impending budget cuts. Elias continues to painstakingly build his digital altars, entirely unaware that the stillness around him is not the silent "amen" of fellow believers, but the muted preamble to a bureaucratic betrayal he will never see coming.
